subtitle.en: Say what you did yesterday or last week
subtitle.tx: Kecha, o'tgan hafta nima qilganingizni aytish

body.en: The Uzbek simple past is the verb stem + -di + a personal ending: bor-di-m (I went), bor-di-ng (you went), bor-di (he/she went), bor-di-k (we went), bor-di-ngiz (you went, formal or plural), bor-di-lar (they went). Unlike English, there are no irregular past forms: every verb follows this pattern. It is always written -di, though after k, p, s, t it often sounds like -ti: ketdim (I left) sounds like 'kettim'.

The -di past reports a single, finished event: Kecha dengizga bordim = Yesterday I went to the sea. For something you used to do again and again, Uzbek uses -ar edi, usually fused into -ardi/-rdi: borardim = I used to go. It matches English 'used to' or 'would'. For a state in the past, use edi (was): Sovuq edi = It was cold.

examples: As a child, I used to go to the sea.
Yesterday I went to the sea.

body.en: To place an action in the past, use time words such as kecha (yesterday), o'tgan hafta (last week), o'tgan yili (last year) and bir necha kun oldin (a few days ago). Oldin works like English 'ago' and comes after the amount of time: ikki kun oldin = two days ago. Time words usually go at the start of the sentence.

body.en: Where English puts a preposition before the noun, Uzbek puts a postposition after it: do'stim bilan (with my friend), sen uchun (for you), darsdan keyin (after the lesson), ovqatdan oldin (before the meal). Keyin (after) and oldin (before) need the noun in -dan.

-ga marks where you are going and -dan where you come from: Rimga boraman = I'm going to Rome, Amerikadan kelaman = I come from America. English uses separate words (to, from); Uzbek just adds the ending to the place name. After k the ending becomes -ka and after q it becomes -qa: qishloqqa = to the village.

subtitle.en: At the doctor's, at the pharmacy, health

body.en: To say something hurts, Uzbek makes the body part the subject, gives it a possessive ending and adds the verb og'rimoq (to hurt), usually in the present continuous: boshim og'riyapti = my head hurts. Where English often says 'I have a headache' or 'I have a sore throat', Uzbek always says 'my head is hurting', 'my throat is hurting'.

To say you must or need to do something, put the verb in the -(i)sh form, add a possessive ending and finish with kerak: dam olishim kerak = I need to rest (lit. 'my resting is necessary'). Without the possessive it becomes a general rule for everyone: dam olish kerak = one should rest. Add -mi for a question: dori ichishim kerakmi? = do I need to take medicine?

examples: One should drink a lot of water.

body.en: Uzbek has no word for 'who', 'that' or 'which'. Instead the verb takes -gan (past) or -adigan/-ydigan (present or habitual) and goes BEFORE the noun it describes: men o'qigan kitob = the book that I read (lit. 'I-read book'); bu yerda ishlaydigan qiz = the girl who works here (lit. 'here-working girl'). English puts the description after the noun; Uzbek puts it in front.

Ability and possibility are expressed with the verb stem + -a (-y after a vowel) + olmoq, which takes the personal ending: gapira olaman = I can speak, bora olmayman = I can't go. One form covers both English 'can' and 'be able to'; the negative goes on olmoq.

body.en: The ending -ib (-b after a vowel) links two actions done by the same person, one after the other. Only the last verb carries the tense and the person: uyga borib, ovqat pishirdim = I went home and cooked (lit. 'having gone home, I cooked'). In English you would usually join the two verbs with 'and'.

An object pronoun is the full pronoun + -ni: meni (me), seni (you), uni (him/her/it), bizni (us), sizni (you, formal or plural), ularni (them). Like everything else, it comes before the verb: Men uni taniyman = I know him. Some verbs take -ga instead of -ni: menga qo'ng'iroq qil = call me (lit. 'make a call to me').

body.en: To say 'bigger', 'more beautiful' and so on, add -roq to the adjective: katta → kattaroq (bigger), chiroyli → chiroyliroq (more beautiful). The thing you compare with takes -dan, which does the job of English 'than': Bu uy o'shadan kattaroq = this house is bigger than that one. There are no irregular forms like 'good → better': yaxshi → yaxshiroq.

For the superlative, put eng in front of the adjective: eng katta (the biggest), eng yaxshi (the best). There is no 'the' and no ending to add. To say 'very', use juda: juda chiroyli (very beautiful).

body.en: Uzbek usually talks about the future with the ordinary present-future tense: boraman = I go / I will go. To stress an intention, use -moqchi + personal ending: bormoqchiman = I'm going to go / I intend to go, o'qimoqchiman = I intend to study. A third form, -(y)ajak (borajak = will go), is formal and bookish; you will meet it more in writing than in speech. 'It will be' is bo'ladi.

Conditions are built with the verb in -sa + personal ending, often with agar (if) at the start: Agar vaqtim bo'lsa, boraman = If I have time, I'll go. Agar is optional, since -sa alone already means 'if'. As in English, the other half of the sentence usually uses the present-future: Agar yomg'ir yog'sa, uyda qolaman = If it rains, I'll stay home.

body.en: Uzbek usually reports what someone said by repeating their exact words and closing the quote with deb (lit. 'saying') or dedi (he/she said): «Kelaman», dedi = He said he's coming (lit. '"I'll come," he said'). Unlike English, you don't shift the person or the tense. For a reported question, the clause takes a verb form + -ni: Qayerda ekanimni so'radi = He asked where I was.

With strangers and older people, use siz and the polite imperative in -ing/-ng: keling (come), o'tiring (have a seat), ayting (tell me). Marhamat means 'please, go ahead' or 'here you are'. English shows politeness with words like 'please' and 'sir'; Uzbek builds it into the verb. A letter often ends with Hurmat bilan (Sincerely, lit. 'with respect').
